children: Wall Street is getting nervous about artificial intelligence. For cybersecurity companies, that is proving good for business.

Data-security company Cyera has raised $400 million from Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, the private markets arm of the banking giant's asset-management division. The investment, an extension of a June Series G funding round that valued the New York-based company at $12 billion, comes as investors continue to pour capital into cybersecurity firms, expecting them to benefit from the risks created by advanced AI models.
The deal brings Cyera's total fundraising since June 2025 to $1.94 billion, an unusually strong financing run during which the company has also become an aggressive acquirer.

Big funding rounds have become increasingly common in cybersecurity, but Cyera's recent haul stands out even in a sector awash with capital. Cybersecurity and privacy startups raised $10.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, according to Crunchbase, with more than 20 companies raising rounds of at least $100 million during the period.

The enthusiasm extends deep into public markets. Cybersecurity stocks surged on Sept. 14 after prominent AI industry figures warned about the systemic risks posed by frontier models and called for a slower pace of development. CrowdStrike Holdings, Zscaler, and Palo Alto Networks all saw double-digit percentage gains, even as the S&P 500 fell 0.5% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite dropped 0.6%.

Much of that rally held through the end of the week. The First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF, which tracks the largest vendors in the sector, jumped 6% on Sept. 14 and retained nearly all of its gains through Friday.
"The urgency in the market for solutions has grown 10-fold," said Yotam Segev, chief executive and co-founder of Cyera.

Segev said investor enthusiasm mirrors demand from corporate customers, noting Cyera recently signed its first client spending more than $10 million annually with the firm. Still, he acknowledged much of the potential market remains years away from full adoption. Companies buying today represent innovators and early adopters, Segev said, while others may not be ready to make similar commitments for several years.

The latest capital injection was driven more by the opportunity to bring Goldman Sachs on as a strategic investor than by an immediate need for cash, Segev said. Discussions occurred alongside the June financing, but internal processes delayed the funding until now.

The new funding nevertheless gives Cyera firepower in dealmaking. Earlier this month, the company completed a $1 billion cash-and-stock acquisition of Oasis Security, a firm specializing in managing nonhuman identities such as AI agents and automated software tools.

Segev said Cyera plans to stay alert for M&A opportunities, and while internal engineering will drive most product development, the company continues to evaluate targets that could expand its data-security platform.
"We want to be in a position to choose the right companies to expand the Cyera portfolio," he said.

Unfettered access to private capital also gives Cyera flexibility over the timing of an initial public offering. Segev said the company has its "sights on going public" and is taking steps to ensure IPO readiness, but emphasized there is little immediate urgency.
"We can and we might," Segev said. "But whether or not that happens, it definitely seems there are other avenues that we can continue to grow and proceed in."
